messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Rohan, a 58-year-old South Asian man, had always been proud of his work as a bomb disposal technician. He took comfort in knowing that he was making a difference, keeping people safe from harm. However, his life took a drastic turn when his young daughter, Sophia, fell critically ill with a rare blood disorder. The hospital became Rohan's second home as he watched his little girl fight for her life. The smell of antiseptic and the sight of medical equipment still haunt him to this day. He recalls the countless nights spent sleeping in the hospital chair beside Sophia's bed, the sound of beeping machines and muffled conversations etched in his memory. The visual image of needles and drips is forever seared into his mind - a constant reminder of those harrowing days. As Sophia slowly recovered, Rohan thought he had begun to heal as well. However, being around children now triggers an overwhelming sense of anxiety within him. He avoids social gatherings, family events, and even simple outings with friends who have kids. What frightened him most was the feeling of helplessness that lingered long after the hospital stay ended - a constant fear that he couldn't protect those he loved from harm. Rohan's sleep patterns began to deteriorate as he found himself lying awake at night, vigilant for any sign of danger. His body would react with intense physical tension whenever something reminded him of Sophia's illness - the sound of an ambulance siren or the sight of a hospital building in the distance. He was certain that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy, losing control of his own mind. Memories of those traumatic days still linger, triggered without warning by the smallest sensory cue. The smell of disinfectant wafting through the air would instantly transport him back to Sophia's hospital room, reliving every detail with vivid intensity - the beeping machines, the sterile sheets, and the soft hum of the ventilator. His memories are mostly visual, a collage of pictures that refuse to fade. Rohan began to believe he was weak for not being able to cope better with his emotions. He felt like he was stuck in this perpetual state of hypervigilance, unable to shake off the fear that something terrible would happen again. As time went by, Rohan became increasingly withdrawn, avoiding social interactions and even conversations about Sophia's illness. At work, colleagues noticed a change in him - a once-sharp technician now hesitant and on edge. His marriage began to suffer as well, his wife struggling to understand why he couldn't simply 'get over' the past. The strain was taking its toll, and Rohan knew he needed help. What finally brought him to seek therapy was the realization that his avoidance behaviors were no longer sustainable - he couldn't keep living in a state of constant fear. As he sat in the therapist's office, Rohan hesitated to share his story, afraid of being judged or deemed 'crazy'. Yet, something about the quiet, non-judgmental space allowed him to begin opening up. He spoke haltingly at first, recounting fragments of those hospital days and the memories that still haunted him. With each passing session, Rohan began to confront his fears, slowly unraveling the web of negative appraisals that had held him captive for so long. What he hopes for most is to learn to manage his triggers, to quiet the constant threat monitor in his mind and find a way back to living life without the suffocating grip of fear. For Rohan, seeking help was the first tentative step towards reclaiming control - a journey that promises to be arduous but ultimately healing.
